title: Books, bikes, and The Burbs: These are Ars staff’s holiday gift picks for 2026
originalTitle: Books, bikes, and The Burbs: These are Ars staff’s holiday gift picks for 2026
content:
– Nick Indge

Under $300

Trek BellBeats digital bike bell and speaker – $125
One of the great things about cycling is the chance to be alone with my thoughts—just me and my bike. But that can be too much of a good thing on longer zone 2 rides and centuries. Sporting the size and shape of an old-school bicycle bell, the Trek BellBeats is a safer alternative to donning headphones while on the bike.

BellBeats pair with your phone via Bluetooth and will play music at a volume loud enough to enjoy your tunes or hear navigation prompts, but they are not so loud that the music drowns out traffic (or the radar on your bike computer). They can be mounted on just about any non-aero handlebars, charge over USB-C, and offer up to six hours of playtime. And as a bonus, they double as a bicycle bell.

– Eric Bangeman

Fractal Design Scape – $160

I use Bluetooth headphones most of the time, but frustratingly, they don’t work with voice chat on the PlayStation 5, and I needed a good-quality headset for my Friday night multiplayer gaming sessions.

I’ve always liked Fractal Design’s PC cases, so I decided to roll the dice on their affordable-for-the-quality, over-ear headphones. They support Bluetooth, but they also have a USB dongle, so they can be used for voice chat on game consoles, too.

I was surprised by how much I like them, and despite buying them just for the PS5, I’ve ended up using them in other contexts. Part of that is because they’re very comfortable, and the design avoids my glasses frames well.

I also like that, although they are gaming headphones with all the expected bells and whistles for that, they don’t have an over-the-top design.

If you’re in the market for mid-range wireless gaming headphones that look like something you could actually wear in public without embarrassment, these fit the bill so far.

– Samuel Axon

Povec C1 Performance Sunglasses – $250
Photochromic sunglasses are incredibly useful for outdoor workouts. Two of the most popular bike trails near me run through forest preserves, and the lighting changes steadily as the forest canopy closes in or spreads out. My default sunglasses are a cheap, $28 pair from Rockbros.

Unlike other photochromic glasses, which change tints via a pokey chemical reaction, the Povec C1 uses a battery to switch between tints in a second. All the rider (or runner) needs to do is swipe the right temple and the lenses will darken or lighten almost instantaneously. The C1 charges via a small USB-C port, and the Povec claims 28 days of battery life with four hours of daily usage. I’ve used them off and on for about six weeks and have only had to charge them once.

The C1 comes in three frame colors and either Green Revo or Gold Revo glasses and is an excellent stocking stuffer for the runner, cyclist, or skier in your life.

– Eric Bangeman

$300 and over

Garmin Varia RCT715 radar camera tail light – $300
Last spring, a friend of mine was the victim of a hit-and-run while on a ride. Although she wasn’t seriously hurt, her brand-new bike was totaled. The driver got an unwelcome surprise a couple of days later when the police knocked on his front door and arrested him. My friend was riding with a Garmin Varia RCT715, a combination taillight and radar with a camera. The 1080p/30 fps camera captured the car’s license plate, making it possible for the police to identify the driver.

More than 90 percent of my riding is on roads, and I don’t feel fully comfortable without my Varia. I have it paired with my Garmin Edge 1050 bike computer, but it will work with most other brands via ANT+. The Varia detects approaching vehicles at 140 meters, and I have it set to record video starting when a car is detected and for 30 seconds after it passes. Battery life is up to six hours, depending on whether the taillight is solid or flashing, and video is saved on a 16GB microSD memory card.

– Eric Bangeman

Hiplock DX1000 Bike Lock – $380

My YouTube algorithm has recently fed me videos of testers using an angle grinder to cut through decent bike locks in under a minute. I’ve never seen an angle grinder-assisted theft in person, but I’ve seen enough heaps of bike parts around town to know people’s rides are getting jacked somewhere. As someone known to be neurotic about leaving my bike outside my purview, I’m looking for added security measures to ease my stress.

Enter the Hiplok, which, according to the tests I’ve watched, will turn multiple angle-grinder blades to dust. Do bike thieves carry several discs, and will they spend about 15 minutes trying to break this lock? I don’t know, but I have my doubts. At nearly $400, it’s about as expensive as it gets to secure your ride, but when your bike tops $5,000, it’s probably worth the added theft deterrence and peace of mind.

– Jacob May

AYN Odin 3 – $767

Santa left this one last year, and the rest of my handheld collection has felt neglected since. Sporting a Snapdragon 8 Elite (now dubbed the Dragonwing Q8) chip, excellent ergonomics, and a 6-inch 120Hz AMOLED screen, it’s the perfect balance between size and horsepower. The Android unit is capable enough to play most anything you can throw at it, without the bulk of a Steam Deck or the bloat of a Windows handheld. Thanks to things like Proton, FEX translation, and software like DroidDeck or GameNative, there isn’t much I can’t use it for. Streaming consoles or PC gaming? Check. Access to Steam, GOG, Epic, Rockstar libraries? Check. High-end native Android gaming? Yup. Emulate anything under the sun? You’re covered there, too. The latest Odin 3 Portal hardware revision gets a larger 7-inch screen and a base RAM configuration of 12GB over the original model’s 8GB. I may have to ask Mr. Claus about an upgrade…

– Nick Indge
